# Summary {#part-infrastructure-summary .unnumbered}

The infrastructure part went below the model. It began with accelerator bandwidth, then the software layer in between: automatic differentiation and the frameworks built around it, then compilers and kernels. In the kernel layer, cost is often set by the bytes moved rather than the FLOPs performed, and applications come to depend on the libraries and tools one vendor has accumulated over many years, which makes moving to other hardware expensive. From there it covered cluster orchestration, data infrastructure, the compute frontier, silicon manufacturing, power, and failure at scale.

The binding limit is rarely the one on the model card. It may be HBM, a network tier, a power interconnect, an export rule, a checkpoint system, or a failure distribution. These form a changing set of physical and operational constraints, and a design that ignores them does not run.

This part leaves open whether advanced packaging, HBM, and grid interconnection can grow on the schedule the training roadmaps assume. Export rules, fab capacity, and a utility queue measured in years decide the answer; chip design does not. Other limits do not depend on hardware supply. Additional HBM does not create training data, a faster interconnect does not measure how capable the resulting model is, and neither lowers the cost of checking the claims a model produces. Part X takes up those limits, which sit above the machine rather than below it.
